name: Thermal efficiency
seoTitle: Thermal efficiency Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Thermal efficiency: work out net work output (Wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ) from the hot reservoir temperature and the cold reservoir temperature. A free physics calculator…
summary: Supply the hot reservoir temperature, the cold reservoir temperature, the heat received and the heat rejected and the Thermal efficiency calculator solves for net work output (Wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Thermal efficiency calculator work?
sections.html:
The Thermal efficiency calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports net work output (Wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of heat engine and the energy units); then you type in the hot reservoir temperature (Tₕ), the cold reservoir temperature (Tc), the heat received (Qiₙ) and the heat rejected (qₒuₜ).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Thermal efficiency calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Net work output (Wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ)=heat received (Qiₙ) × thermal efficiency (ηₜₕ)
Heat rejected (Qₒuₜ)=heat received (Qiₙ) − net work output (Wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ)
Heat rejected (Qₒuₜ)=heat received (Qiₙ) × (1 − thermal efficiency (ηₜₕ))
Net work output (wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ)=thermal efficiency (ηₜₕ) × heat received (qiₙ)
Net work output (wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ)=heat received (qiₙ) − heat rejected (qₒuₜ)
Heat received (qiₙ)=-heat rejected (qₒuₜ) ÷ (thermal efficiency (ηₜₕ) − 1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Type of heat engine set to Reversible (Carnot heat engine), Energy units set to Total energy, Heat received (Qiₙ) = 10 J and Thermal efficiency (ηₜₕ) = 10 %. Working through the relationship above gives Heat rejected (Qₒuₜ) = 9 J and Net work output (Wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ) = 1 J.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Heat rejected (Qₒuₜ) = 9 J and Net work output (Wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ) = 1 J should be roughly the size you expected from Type of heat engine set to Reversible (Carnot heat engine) and Energy units set to Total energy.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • %, opening in percent
  • Energy, opening in joules
  • Energy, opening in joules
  • Energy, opening in joules
  • %, opening in percent
  • Energy per mass, opening in kilojoules per kilogram

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Thermal efficiency calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the hot reservoir temperature, the cold reservoir temperature and the heat received — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Thermal efficiency calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns net work output (Wₙₑₜ,ₒuₜ), derived from the hot reservoir temperature, the cold reservoir temperature and the heat received. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Thermal efficiency calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the hot reservoir temperature, the cold reservoir temperature, the heat received and the heat rejected, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter hot reservoir temperature (Tₕ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Hot reservoir temperature (Tₕ) opens in kelvins and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Heat rejected (Qₒuₜ) = 9 J. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Thermal efficiency calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
